The night sky has always been humanity’s oldest storybook. Long before we had telescopes or equations, people lay on their backs and traced patterns among the stars, inventing myths that explained birth, death, and the seasons. Those same pinpricks of light still hang above us, indifferent to our calendars and deadlines, yet they continue to pull at something deep and restless inside us.

I often think about how strange it is that we can feel lonely while standing under a sky that contains more stars than there are grains of sand on every beach on Earth. The scale is almost insulting. Our entire history—wars, loves, inventions, heartbreaks—occupies less than a blink of cosmic time. And yet that same vastness is what makes curiosity feel like a form of courage. Every time someone points a new instrument at a distant galaxy or asks a better question about black holes or consciousness, they are refusing to be small.

Curiosity is not a luxury reserved for scientists. It is the quiet refusal to accept that the world is finished. It lives in a child turning over a rock, in a cook inventing a new sauce, in anyone who pauses long enough to wonder why the light hits the leaves that particular way at dusk. When we stop asking, we shrink. When we keep asking, the universe—somehow—feels a little less empty and a little more like home.

So tonight, if the sky is clear, step outside. Look up. Let the ancient light reach you. Then ask one more question, even if no answer comes. That is enough.
